analogy.p: Picture pupils in a school. In **assembly** (solid) everyone is sitting in neat rows, shoulder to shoulder, able to fidget but not to move away. In the **corridor at the end of lesson** (liquid) pupils are packed close together but jostling past one another, and the whole crowd flows. On the **field at break** (gas) pupils run in every direction, far apart, colliding only occasionally. Being 'held in a row' is like strong forces; if the head teacher (energy) lets everyone get up, the rows break down. It breaks down because real particles are attracted by electrical forces rather than by rules, because pupils choose where to go whereas particles move randomly, and because a school has a limited number of different groups whereas particles do not.
analogy.t: A school: assembly, corridor and playground

bullets: Describe the **arrangement, movement and energy** of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Name and explain **melting, freezing, boiling (evaporating), condensing** (and sublimation as an extension).
Explain that the **amount of energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles**.
Explain that the **nature of the particles** (atoms, molecules, ions) and the **type of bonding** decide the strength of those forces.
Use **melting point and boiling point data** to decide whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature.
Use the **state symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq)** in chemical equations.
Evaluate the **limitations of the particle model**, for example that it shows particles as solid spheres with no forces.
This is a **Paper 1** topic and examiners love 4 to 6 mark questions that make you link bonding, structure and melting point.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8462 section 4.2.2 asks you to link the **state of a substance at a given temperature** to the **strength of the forces between its particles**, and then to link those forces to the **type of bonding and structure**. You must be able to use the **particle model** to describe solids, liquids and gases, name the **changes of state**, explain what happens to the particles during each one, **predict the state** of a substance from its melting and boiling points, use **state symbols** in equations, and describe the **limitations of the simple particle model**. The key idea running through everything is that **the stronger the forces between particles, the more energy is needed to overcome them, so the higher the melting point and boiling point**.

bullets: **Solid**: particles are **very close together** in a **regular arrangement** (a lattice); they **vibrate about fixed positions** and cannot move from place to place. Solids have a **fixed shape and fixed volume** and **cannot be compressed**.

**Liquid**: particles are **close together** in a **random arrangement**; they can **move around and slide past each other**. Liquids have a **fixed volume but no fixed shape** (they take the shape of the bottom of the container) and are **almost impossible to compress**.

**Gas**: particles are **far apart** and arranged **randomly**; they move **quickly in all directions**. Gases have **no fixed shape or volume** (they fill the container) and **can be compressed** because of the large spaces between particles.

**Density** is highest in solids and liquids (particles close together) and **very low in gases** (particles far apart). Water and a few others are exceptions where ice is less dense than liquid water, but you do not need to explain this at GCSE.
**Forces of attraction** are **strongest in solids**, weaker in liquids and **almost negligible in gases**.
The **kinetic energy of the particles** (and so how fast they move) **increases from solid to liquid to gas**.
Higher tier thinking: at any one temperature, particles in a substance have a range of energies; the **average kinetic energy is what is related to temperature**.
core.p: Matter exists in three main **states of matter**: **solid, liquid and gas**. Which state a substance is in at a particular temperature depends on how much **energy** its particles have compared with the strength of the **forces of attraction** between them. In a solid the forces hold the particles in fixed positions; in a liquid the particles have enough energy to move past one another but not to escape completely; in a gas the particles have so much energy that the forces between them are almost irrelevant and they spread out to fill the container. Particles in all three states are in constant motion, but the type of motion is different in each.

bullets: **Solid** diagram: circles in **regular rows**, **touching**. Do not leave big gaps and do not draw them randomly.
**Liquid** diagram: circles **touching or nearly touching but in a random pattern**; some small gaps are allowed because liquids are slightly less tightly packed than solids.
**Gas** diagram: circles **far apart** (several diameters between them) and **random**. Do not draw a gas as a tidy pattern.
Draw **all the circles the same size** unless the question uses different elements.
Do not draw **lines or arrows joining particles** unless the question asks for bonds, because the simple particle diagram does not show bonds.
In a mixture of gases, show **separate particles**; in a diatomic gas such as oxygen (O2), the particle is a **pair of joined atoms**.
To show **movement**, short arrows of different lengths can be used; **longer arrows mean faster particles**.
Mark scheme language: 'particles are in a **regular pattern**', 'particles are **close together**', 'particles **vibrate about fixed positions**'.
core.h: Particle diagrams and drawing them in the exam
core.p: Examiners often ask you to **draw or interpret a particle diagram**. A particle is drawn as a small circle. To earn marks you must show the correct **spacing**, **arrangement** and, where asked, the idea of **movement**. A solid is drawn as circles **touching in neat rows**, a liquid as circles **touching but in a jumbled random pattern with some small gaps**, and a gas as circles **well spaced and random**. If a question tells you the diagram is of a compound or mixture, you may need to use two different kinds of circle (for example shaded and unshaded) to show different types of atom.

bullets: **Melting**: solid to liquid at the **melting point**. The particles gain enough energy to **overcome the forces holding them in fixed positions**.
**Freezing**: liquid to solid at the **freezing point** (which is **the same temperature as the melting point** for a pure substance).
**Boiling**: liquid to gas at the **boiling point**; bubbles of vapour form **throughout the liquid** and particles gain enough energy to **overcome the forces between them completely**.
**Condensing**: gas to liquid at the **boiling point** (same temperature as boiling for a pure substance); the particles lose energy and the forces pull them together.
**Sublimation** (extension): solid straight to gas without becoming liquid, for example **solid carbon dioxide ('dry ice')** and **iodine**. The reverse is called **deposition**.
Changes of state are **physical changes, not chemical reactions**: no bonds inside molecules are broken or made; only **forces between particles** are overcome.
**Mass stays the same** because no particles are lost, but **volume changes**, especially for liquid to gas where the volume increases enormously.

A **pure substance** melts and boils at **sharp, fixed temperatures**; an **impure substance** melts over a **range of temperatures** and at a **lower** melting point than the pure substance (a way to test purity).
core.h: Changes of state: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing
core.p: A **change of state** is a **physical change**: the particles are the same before and after, only their arrangement and energy change, so **no new substance is made** and the change is **reversible**. **Melting** is solid to liquid, **freezing** is liquid to solid, **boiling** (or evaporating) is liquid to gas, and **condensing** is gas to liquid. Melting and boiling need **energy transferred to the particles** (they are **endothermic**), whereas freezing and condensing **release energy** to the surroundings (they are **exothermic**). **Mass is conserved** during every change of state because the number of particles does not change.

bullets: **Sloping section**: energy goes to **raising the kinetic energy** of the particles, so **temperature increases**.
**Flat section at the melting point**: solid and liquid are **both present**; energy is used to **break the forces holding particles in the lattice**.
**Flat section at the boiling point**: liquid and gas are both present; energy is used to **completely separate the particles**.
The boiling point flat section is **longer** than the melting point flat section because **much more energy is needed to separate particles completely** than to let them slide past each other.
On a **cooling curve** the same shape is seen in reverse; flat sections occur at the **freezing point** (energy released as forces form) and the **condensing point**.
Reading the graph: the **temperature of a flat section** gives the melting or boiling point; the **time length** of a flat section is proportional to the energy needed (at a steady heating rate).

Common graph question: 'What is happening to the particles between points B and C?' Answer: 'the solid is **melting**; energy is used to **overcome the forces between particles** so temperature stays constant.'
The **stronger the forces**, the **higher** the temperature of the flat sections.
core.h: Energy changes and the heating curve
core.p: When a substance is heated steadily, its temperature does not rise all the time. A **heating curve** (temperature against time) shows **sloping sections** where the substance is warming and **flat sections** where it is changing state. In the sloping sections the energy supplied increases the **kinetic energy of the particles**, so the temperature rises. In the flat sections the energy supplied is used to **overcome the forces of attraction between the particles** rather than to make them move faster, so the temperature stays **constant** until the change of state is complete. The first flat section is at the **melting point** and the second, higher flat section is at the **boiling point**.

bullets: **Boiling**: occurs at a **fixed temperature** (the boiling point); bubbles form **throughout** the liquid.
**Evaporation**: occurs at **any temperature** below the boiling point; **only at the surface**; no bubbles.
Evaporation is **faster** when the liquid is **warmer**, the **surface area is larger**, there is a **draught** and the air is **dry**.
Particles that escape during evaporation are the **most energetic**, so the liquid **cools**.
Substances with **weak intermolecular forces** evaporate easily and are called **volatile**, for example ethanol and propanone.
Evaporation is used in **crystallisation** (removing solvent) and in **simple distillation**, which uses boiling and then condensing.
core.p: Liquids can turn into gas in two ways. **Boiling** happens only at the **boiling point**, takes place **throughout the liquid** (bubbles form inside), and needs a continuous energy supply. **Evaporation** happens at **any temperature below the boiling point**, only at the **surface**, and occurs when the fastest-moving particles near the surface have enough energy to **escape the attraction of the other particles**. Evaporation is why puddles dry up and why sweating cools you down: the particles that escape are the **highest-energy ones**, so the **average energy (and temperature) of the liquid left behind falls**. The AQA specification uses boiling and evaporating together for liquid to gas, but understanding the difference helps you avoid mistakes.

bullets: **Strength of forces** is the first idea: **stronger forces mean more energy needed, so higher melting and boiling points**.
**Number of forces** matters too: in a giant structure **billions of bonds** act through the whole structure; in small molecules only weak forces between separate molecules act.
Compare **like with like**: always say what type of structure each substance has before you compare their melting points.
The melting point depends on the **energy needed to separate the particles or lattice**, not on how heavy the particles are (though bigger molecules do have stronger intermolecular forces).
Typical orders: **simple molecular (lowest) < ionic and metallic (high) < giant covalent (usually very high)**.
Use the exact phrase **'a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong ...'** in answers about high melting points.
Use the phrase **'little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces'** for simple molecules.
core.h: Why different substances have different melting and boiling points
core.p: Substances differ enormously: methane melts at about **-182 °C** while diamond sublimes above **3500 °C**. This happens because what must be **overcome** during a change of state is different in each type of substance. For simple molecules it is the **weak intermolecular forces**; for ionic compounds it is the **strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions**; for metals it is the **electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons**; and for giant covalent substances it is the **strong covalent bonds** themselves. The more energy needed to do this, the higher the melting point and boiling point. Always name **exactly what is overcome** when you answer, because a vague answer such as 'it takes more energy' does not score.

bullets: **High melting and boiling points** (sodium chloride melts at **801 °C**): a lot of energy is needed to overcome the **strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions**.
**Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity** because the ions are **in fixed positions** and cannot move to carry charge.
**Molten and dissolved (aqueous) ionic compounds conduct** because the **ions are free to move** and carry the electric charge.
Many ionic compounds are **soluble in water** and are **brittle**: a blow shifts layers so like charges line up and repel, and the crystal shatters (an extension idea).

The **higher the charges on the ions** and the **smaller the ions**, the stronger the attraction. For example, magnesium oxide (Mg2+ and O2-) has a **much higher melting point (about 2850 °C)** than sodium chloride (Na+ and Cl-).
Do **not** say 'ionic bonds are broken between molecules': there are **no molecules** in an ionic compound.
Do **not** say 'ions are free to move' for the solid.
Link to topic: **electrolysis** (4.4) only works when the ionic compound is **molten or in solution**.
core.p: **Ionic compounds** such as sodium chloride and magnesium oxide have a **giant ionic lattice** in which positive and negative **ions** are arranged in a regular repeating pattern. Every ion is held by **strong electrostatic forces of attraction** in all directions to the oppositely charged ions around it. These forces act throughout the whole lattice, so a **large amount of energy** is needed to separate the ions. This explains why ionic compounds are **solid at room temperature** and have **high melting points and boiling points**. When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved, the ions are able to move, which allows it to **conduct electricity**.

bullets: **Low melting and boiling points** because of **weak intermolecular forces** that need little energy to overcome.
**Do not conduct electricity** (solid, liquid or gas) because molecules have **no overall charge** and there are **no delocalised electrons or free ions**.

As **molecules get bigger**, the **intermolecular forces get stronger**, so more energy is needed and the **melting and boiling points rise**. This is why the hydrocarbon boiling points increase along the series: methane is a gas, octane a liquid and long chains are waxy solids.
Common error: saying 'the **covalent bonds** break when it melts'. Correct: **intermolecular forces** are overcome, **covalent bonds stay intact** (water is still H2O when it boils).
Many simple molecular substances are **poor conductors of heat** and are **soft or brittle solids**.
Examples to quote: **water, ammonia, carbon dioxide, methane, iodine, chlorine, hydrogen chloride**.
Formulae show small numbers of atoms, for example **H2O, CH4, CO2, O2**.
Higher tier thinking: the intermolecular forces are not bonds and are much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why molecular substances are so easy to melt.
core.p: **Simple molecular substances** such as water, methane, carbon dioxide and oxygen are made of **small molecules** whose atoms are joined by **strong covalent bonds**. However, the forces **between separate molecules**, called **intermolecular forces**, are **weak**. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, it is only the **weak intermolecular forces that are overcome**; the **covalent bonds inside each molecule do not break**. Only a small amount of energy is needed, so these substances have **low melting and boiling points** and are usually **gases or liquids at room temperature**.

bullets: **Very high melting points** (silicon dioxide about **1700 °C**; diamond above **3500 °C**) because **strong covalent bonds** must be broken.
**Insoluble in water** and most solvents because the bonds are too strong to be separated.
**Most do not conduct electricity** (no delocalised or free electrons or ions), but **graphite does conduct** because each carbon has **one delocalised electron**.
Silicon dioxide is made of **silicon and oxygen atoms** in a giant lattice with a **ratio of 1 : 2** (formula SiO2). It is **the main compound in sand**.
Do not call them 'molecules': say **'giant covalent structure'** or **'giant covalent lattice'**.
Exam answer: 'It has a **giant covalent structure** with **many strong covalent bonds**, which need **a lot of energy** to break, so it has a **high melting point**.'
core.p: **Giant covalent structures** such as diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide (silica) are made of **millions of atoms** joined together by **strong covalent bonds** in a continuous network. To melt or boil them you must **break many strong covalent bonds**, which requires a **very large amount of energy**. They therefore have **very high melting and boiling points** and are **solid at room temperature**. Their properties vary: diamond is very hard and does not conduct, whereas graphite is slippery and conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons. These are covered in detail in the carbon structures topic (4.2.3).

bullets: **Metals**: high mp and bp because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the **strong electrostatic forces between positive ions and delocalised electrons**.
**Metals conduct** electricity and heat because the **delocalised electrons can move** and carry charge or energy through the metal.
**Metals are malleable** because the layers of ions can **slide over each other** without breaking the bonding.
**Polymers**: long molecules, so intermolecular forces are **stronger than those in small molecules** (more points of contact along the chains), so they are **solid at room temperature**.
Polymers do not conduct (no free charged particles) and soften or melt at **moderate temperatures** compared with giant structures.
For polymers, still say **'the covalent bonds do not break; intermolecular forces are overcome'**.
Key contrast: polymer melting needs **more energy than small molecules** but **less than giant covalent or ionic structures**.
core.p: **Metals** have a **giant metallic structure**: a regular lattice of **positive metal ions** surrounded by a 'sea' of **delocalised electrons**. The **strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons** (called **metallic bonding**) holds the structure together, so most metals have **high melting and boiling points** and are solid at room temperature. Mercury is the well-known exception that is liquid because its metallic bonding is unusually weak. **Polymers** are very large molecules (thousands of atoms) made of long chains, and although the atoms in each chain are joined by strong covalent bonds, the **intermolecular forces between chains are relatively strong** compared with those between small molecules. This is why most polymers are **solids at room temperature**.

bullets: **Below melting point** = **solid**.
**Between melting and boiling point** = **liquid** (the temperature must be strictly between the two).
**Above boiling point** = **gas**.
**At the melting point exactly** = a **mixture of solid and liquid** at equilibrium (the substance is changing state).
Draw a **number line** with the melting and boiling points on it and mark the given temperature.
Example: oxygen mp -218 °C, bp -183 °C: at 20 °C it is above its boiling point, so it is a **gas**.
Example: bromine mp -7 °C, bp 59 °C: at 20 °C it is between, so a **liquid**; at 100 °C it is a **gas**.
Example: sodium chloride mp 801 °C, bp 1413 °C: at 20 °C a **solid**; at 1000 °C a **liquid**.
To **explain** the state, link the numbers back to forces: 'a high melting point means strong forces between particles'.
core.h: Predicting the state from melting and boiling points
core.p: You are often given a table of melting and boiling points and asked for the **state of a substance at a stated temperature**. Use a simple rule: if the temperature is **below the melting point**, the substance is a **solid**; if it is **between the melting point and boiling point**, it is a **liquid**; if it is **above the boiling point**, it is a **gas**. Room temperature is usually taken as **20 °C** or **25 °C**. Be extremely careful with **negative numbers**: for example, a melting point of **-7 °C** is *below* 20 °C, so the substance has already melted. A number line sketch removes silly mistakes.

bullets: **(s)** = solid, for example Mg(s), CaCO3(s), the precipitate in a precipitation reaction.
**(l)** = liquid, for example H2O(l), Br2(l), a **molten** substance.
**(g)** = gas, for example H2(g), CO2(g), O2(g).
**(aq)** = aqueous solution (**dissolved in water**), for example HCl(aq), NaOH(aq), NaCl(aq).
Example: **Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)**.
Example: **CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)**.
A **precipitate** is an **insoluble solid formed in solution**, shown as (s), for example AgCl(s).
Do not write (aq) for **water itself**; write **H2O(l)**. Do not write (g) for steam unless the question says it is steam.
State symbols are often **worth a mark** in 'write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols' questions.
core.p: In chemical equations **state symbols** show the physical state of each substance: **(s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous**, meaning **dissolved in water**. They are written in brackets directly after the formula, and they give extra information in a balanced equation. **(aq)** is not the same as (l): it means a solution, so a substance that is dissolved in water is (aq), while pure water is (l). State symbols do not change the balancing, but you should add them when the question asks. They are also needed to write **ionic equations** correctly in later topics, because only aqueous ions are written separately.

bullets: **No forces** between particles are shown, yet forces are the whole reason for different melting points.
**Particles are shown as solid spheres**; real atoms have a nucleus and electrons, and ions and molecules are not spherical.
**Particles are all the same size**; real ions and atoms differ in size.
**Gaps are not to scale**: the space between gas particles is really far larger than any diagram can show.
The model does **not show how particles move** or how their energy is distributed.
It does **not show covalent bonds** within molecules, so it cannot show the difference between a molecule and separate atoms.
Good answer shape: 'The model shows ... but a limitation is that it ...'.
Strengths: it **explains changes of state, compressibility of gases, diffusion and expansion**.
core.h: Limitations of the simple particle model
core.p: The particle model is a **simple model** that explains a lot but not everything. Examiners ask you to **evaluate** it, which means stating both what the model does well and where it is inaccurate. The main limitations are that in the diagrams **there are no forces shown between the particles**, that **all particles are shown as solid, inelastic spheres** when they are really atoms, molecules or ions with internal structure, and that **the spaces between particles and the true sizes of particles are not to scale**, especially for gases. The model also cannot show **how particles are bonded** or that bonds inside molecules are different from forces between molecules. Despite these limits, the model is useful for explaining changes of state, pressure, diffusion and density.

bullets: **Distillation and fractional distillation**: separating liquids with different boiling points.
**Hydrocarbons**: longer chain, stronger intermolecular forces, higher boiling point, less volatile.
**Rates**: higher temperature means more energy, so more frequent and more energetic collisions.
**Electrolysis**: ionic compounds only conduct when molten or dissolved.
**Physics link**: specific latent heat is the energy needed to change state without a temperature change.
**Atmosphere**: condensing water vapour made the oceans.
core.h: Linking to other topics and exam strategy
core.p: States of matter connects to many other parts of the course. The same idea of 'overcoming forces between particles' appears in **separation techniques** (distillation uses the different boiling points of liquids), in **crude oil and hydrocarbons** (fractional distillation depends on increasing boiling points as molecules get larger), in **rates of reaction** (particles in a hotter solution have more energy and collide more often) and in **energy changes** (bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic). In physics, the same ideas appear as the **particle model of matter**, **specific latent heat** and **internal energy**.

exam: **1 mark** questions: name a change of state, give a state symbol, or read the state from a table. Check negative numbers carefully.
**2 mark** questions: 'explain why X has a low melting point': 'weak **intermolecular forces** (1) so **little energy** needed to overcome them (1)'.
**'Describe the arrangement and movement'** (typically 2 to 3 marks): give spacing, pattern and movement for each state.
**'Explain' with 3 or 4 marks**: use the chain **structure (giant lattice) → forces between particles (strong electrostatic) → a lot of energy needed → high melting point**.

**6 mark comparison questions**: plan a short paragraph for each substance (type of structure, forces or bonds overcome, relative energy), then a conclusion comparing the two. Quality of written communication counts.
Always say **what is overcome**: 'intermolecular forces', 'strong electrostatic forces between ions', 'strong covalent bonds' or 'electrostatic attraction between ions and delocalised electrons'.
Never say 'bonds break' for simple molecules; say **'intermolecular forces'** or you lose the mark.
**Graph questions**: flat sections = change of state; read the temperature off the y-axis for the melting or boiling point; longer flat = more energy used.
**Limitations of the model (2 marks)**: 'no forces shown between particles' and 'particles shown as solid spheres'.
**State symbols**: put them directly after the formula, with no spaces, for example CO2(g).
Use **command words**: 'state' = short answer, 'describe' = what, 'explain' = why (use because), 'compare' = both substances in each sentence, 'evaluate' = strengths and limitations with a judgement.

mistakes.r: Only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules stay intact.
mistakes.w: Covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance (like water or methane) melts or boils.

mistakes.r: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they cannot move from place to place.
mistakes.w: Particles in a solid do not move at all.

mistakes.r: The particles stay the same size; the spaces between them increase because they have more energy and move faster.
mistakes.w: The particles themselves expand or get bigger when heated or when a solid turns to a gas.

mistakes.r: Ionic compounds have a giant lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions; there are no molecules.
mistakes.w: Ionic compounds have molecules / ionic bonds between molecules.

mistakes.r: They conduct only when molten or dissolved because the ions are then free to move and carry charge; solid ions are fixed.
mistakes.w: Ionic compounds conduct electricity because they contain electrons that move (as in metals).

mistakes.r: It takes more energy because the forces of attraction between particles are stronger (name the forces overcome).
mistakes.w: It takes more energy because the substance is heavier.

mistakes.r: (aq) means dissolved in water; pure water is (l) and other pure liquids are (l).
mistakes.w: Writing (aq) for water or for any liquid.

mistakes.r: Temperature stays constant during a change of state because the energy is used to overcome forces between particles.
mistakes.w: Temperature rises during melting as energy is added.

mistakes.r: 20 °C is above -7 °C, so it has melted; use a number line to compare, especially with negatives.
mistakes.w: A substance with a melting point of -7 °C is a solid at 20 °C.

summary: The specification asks you to describe solids, liquids and gases using the particle model, name and explain the changes of state, predict a substance's state from its melting and boiling points, use state symbols, and explain how the strength of forces between particles (ionic, covalent, metallic or intermolecular) controls the energy needed to change state. It matters because every Paper 1 question on structure and bonding ends up using this reasoning.

terms.d: One of the three physical forms of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
A model in which all matter is made of tiny particles; the arrangement, movement and energy of the particles explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid (the same temperature as the freezing point for a pure substance).
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas throughout the liquid (the same temperature as the condensing point for a pure substance).
The change of state from liquid to solid, in which energy is released to the surroundings.
The change of state from gas to liquid, in which energy is released to the surroundings.
The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.
Weak forces of attraction between separate molecules, overcome when a simple molecular substance melts or boils.
A strong bond formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms; it is not broken when a simple molecular substance changes state.
Forces between oppositely charged particles, such as between positive and negative ions in an ionic lattice.
A regular repeating arrangement of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.
Outer shell electrons in a metal that are free to move through the structure and are not attached to one atom.
A structure of very many atoms joined by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network.
Describes a liquid that evaporates easily because of weak intermolecular forces and a low boiling point.
Symbols written after a formula in an equation to show state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution.
Dissolved in water to form a solution.
A single element or compound not mixed with any other substance, which has sharp melting and boiling points.

worked.ans: (a) Bromine liquid, sodium chloride solid, oxygen gas. (b) Bromine is a gas at 100 °C.
worked.q:
The table shows melting and boiling points. (a) Give the state of each substance at 25 °C. (b) What is the state of bromine at 100 °C? [4 marks]
Substance W: bromine, mp -7 °C, bp 59 °C. X: sodium chloride, mp 801 °C, bp 1413 °C. Y: oxygen, mp -218 °C, bp -183 °C.
steps: Draw a number line for each substance and mark 25 °C.
Bromine: -7 < 25 < 59, so 25 °C lies between the melting and boiling points: liquid.
Sodium chloride: 25 < 801, below the melting point: solid.
Oxygen: 25 > -183, above the boiling point: gas.
Bromine at 100 °C: 100 > 59, above the boiling point: gas.

worked.ans: Sodium chloride has a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. A lot of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so it has a high melting point. Methane is a simple molecular substance whose molecules are held to each other by weak intermolecular forces. Only a little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces (the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break), so methane has a very low melting point. Therefore sodium chloride has a much higher melting point than methane because stronger forces must be overcome.
worked.q: Explain why sodium chloride has a much higher melting point than methane (CH4). [6 marks]
steps: Sodium chloride: describe structure (giant ionic lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions).
State what is overcome: strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.
Link to energy: a lot of energy is needed, so a high melting point (801 °C).
Methane: simple molecular, small molecules with strong covalent bonds inside each molecule.
State what is overcome: weak intermolecular forces between molecules; the covalent bonds do not break.
Link to energy: little energy is needed, so a very low melting point (about -182 °C); finish with a comparison.

worked.q: Write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols for the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid. [3 marks]
steps: Reactants: magnesium is a solid metal, hydrochloric acid is a solution: Mg(s) and HCl(aq).
Products: magnesium chloride is soluble so MgCl2(aq); hydrogen is a gas, H2(g).
Balance: Mg + 2HCl gives MgCl2 + H2; check Cl: 2 on each side, H: 2 on each side.
